title: Iterators and Generators
oneLiner: What a loop really does (IEnumerable and MoveNext, iter and next), writing sequences with yield in both languages, laziness, endless sequences and pipelines, and making your own classes loopable.
keyTakeaway: A method with yield return (C#) or a function with yield (Python) produces a lazy sequence: its body runs only as items are requested, pausing at each yield. That lets you process endless or huge sequences in constant memory, but a Python generator can be read once, and a C# iterator reruns from the top every time it's enumerated.
explanation:
Every foreach and for loop works the same way underneath: it asks the collection for an iterator, an object that hands out one item at a time and remembers its place, and keeps asking until there are no more. In C# the collection is an IEnumerable<T> and the iterator an IEnumerator<T>; in Python they're any object with __iter__ and __next__, and the end is signalled by StopIteration.

The useful part is that you can write your own sequences without building a list. A C# method containing yield return, or a Python function containing yield (a generator), hands back one value at a time, pausing between them with its local variables intact. Nothing runs until the first item is requested, and the rest never runs if nobody asks for it.

That lazy evaluation makes it possible to describe endless sequences (all the natural numbers, every Fibonacci number) and to chain steps into pipelines that read a huge file or stream line by line in constant memory. It also has traps, covered in the questions: generators are one-shot, and an iterator's code runs later than it looks.
